stem: A 70-year-old woman has had 6 months of bad breath and regurgitation of undigested food eaten hours earlier. She sometimes hears gurgling in her neck after swallowing and has coughed at night. She has no heartburn. Examination shows only halitosis.
oneliner: 70F + 6 months of halitosis + regurgitation of undigested food hours later + neck gurgling + nocturnal cough + no heartburn → best first diagnostic test?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate first diagnostic test?

whyNot.B: Passing a scope first risks **perforating a pouch** that causes her **regurgitation of old food, halitosis and neck gurgling**
whyNot.C: Tests muscle pressures but does not show the **pouch** suggested by her **regurgitation and neck gurgling**
whyNot.D: Poorly outlines a hollow pouch that fills with food; her **symptoms after swallowing** need a test that shows the lumen during swallowing
whyNot.E: Tests for acid reflux, and she has **no heartburn**

why: **Regurgitation of undigested food hours later, halitosis and neck gurgling** suggest a Zenker diverticulum. A barium swallow fills and outlines the pouch safely; endoscopy first risks perforating it.

idea.rule: For a suspected pouch or narrowing, show the anatomy with a contrast study before passing an instrument through it.
also: Achalasia: barium swallow shows a bird's-beak, then manometry confirms
Esophageal stricture or web: barium swallow shows the narrowing before endoscopic dilation
Suspected esophageal perforation: water-soluble contrast study, not barium
Zenker pouch lies in the Killian triangle above the cricopharyngeus

stem: A 67-year-old woman comes for a routine health visit. Her mother and her brother both had colon cancer. She feels well and has no rectal bleeding or change in bowel habits. She asks to be screened only with a stool test for blood that she can do at home.
oneliner: 67F + mother and brother with colon cancer + asymptomatic + prefers only a stool blood test → best screening test?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate screening test for this patient?

whyNot.A: The stool test has **low sensitivity** and misses polyps and cancers that do not bleed; she has **two first-degree relatives** with colon cancer
whyNot.B: Used to follow a **known** cancer, not to screen a woman with **no symptoms**
whyNot.C: Less sensitive and cannot remove polyps; her **family history** calls for the most sensitive test
whyNot.D: Cannot remove polyps; with **two first-degree relatives** affected, one test that finds and treats lesions is preferred

why: With **two first-degree relatives** affected she is high risk. A stool blood test has **low sensitivity**, so a negative result falsely reassures when polyps and tumors do not bleed. **Colonoscopy** examines the whole colon and removes polyps at the same visit.

idea.rule: A screening test must be highly sensitive in the people who most need it, because a false negative falsely reassures a high-risk patient.
also: A negative result on a very sensitive test helps rule disease out
A positive stool blood test is followed by colonoscopy, not repeat stool testing
Lynch syndrome: colonoscopy every 1 to 2 years starting in the twenties
Familial adenomatous polyposis: colon surveillance starting in adolescence

stem: A 28-year-old man is taken to the operating room after a car crash with low blood pressure and a rigid abdomen. At laparotomy a deep tear crosses both the right and left lobes of the liver and bleeds briskly. The surgeon wants to cut off the blood flowing into the liver for a few minutes.
oneliner: 28M + car crash + hypotension + rigid abdomen + deep tear of both liver lobes bleeding briskly + inflow must be stopped briefly → which structure is clamped?
ask: Which of the following structures should the surgeon clamp?

whyNot.A: Carries the left and right gastric vessels, not the **inflow to both lobes**
whyNot.B: Holds the ligamentum teres and carries no **inflow to the liver**
whyNot.C: Attaches the liver to the diaphragm and does not carry the **blood entering the liver**
whyNot.E: Carries the short gastric vessels to the stomach, not the **inflow to both lobes** of the liver

why: The **hepatic artery, portal vein and bile duct** run in the free edge of the lesser omentum, the **hepatoduodenal ligament**. Clamping it (Pringle maneuver) stops inflow to both lobes; bleeding that continues suggests injury to the hepatic veins or vena cava.

idea.rule: Know what each peritoneal ligament carries.
also: Hepatoduodenal ligament: portal triad, with the epiploic foramen of Winslow behind it
Falciform ligament: ligamentum teres hepatis (remnant of the umbilical vein)
Gastrosplenic ligament: short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels
Splenorenal ligament: splenic vessels and the tail of the pancreas
